Agent World Model in the Wild:
Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis

Zhaoyang Wang, Qianhui Wu, Haorui Wang, Simon Yu, Baolin Peng Affiliation: UNC-Chapel Hill Affiliation: Microsoft Research Affiliation: Georgia Tech Affiliation: Northeastern University    Canwen Xu, Hao Cheng, Wenlin Yao, Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Jianfeng Gao, Huaxiu Yao Email: zhaoyang@cs.unc.edu~~~qianhuiwu@microsoft.com Project Page   Data & Models   Harbor   Code Affiliation: UNC-Chapel Hill Affiliation: Microsoft Research Affiliation: Independent Researcher
Abstract

Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM’s synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) powered agents are shifting from learning from humans to learning from the world (Silver & Sutton, 2025). Early agents learned from human data, which are expensive to collect and limited by demonstrator’s ability. Recent agents instead gain much of their capability through reinforcement learning (RL) in executable environments (Team et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), making environment supply a key bottleneck. However, training directly in the real world is costly and risky: states are hard to reset, online services change over time, and exploratory actions may have unintended consequences.11 1 For example, see OpenAI’s recent incident report on real-world RL at this url. Manually built environments restore control and verifiability (Yao et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), but remain expensive and hard to scale. Synthetic environments and tasks offer a path to controllable, large-scale online RL.

Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) represent a broad setting for environment synthesis, as they operate across applications, websites, and local files on a personal computer. A single task may be completed through graphical user interface (GUI) interaction, command-line interface (CLI) operations, or calls to model context protocol (MCP) servers, making interface selection and coordination an important capability. Existing synthesis pipelines often target individual interaction modes, including browser use (Zhou, 2026; Wu et al., 2026), tool calling (Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d), and terminal workflows (Li et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Prior CUA work, however, often focuses primarily on GUI interaction (Aggarwal et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). In this paper, we adopt a broader view of computer use spanning common interfaces on a personal computer, since real computer-use tasks are defined by what can be accomplished rather than by a single interaction modality.

Synthesizing environments and tasks for this broader CUA setting introduces challenges beyond prior synthesis work. Existing approaches often synthesize visually simplified applications and build each application as an isolated environment. In contrast, realistic computer use spans a connected digital workspace in which websites, applications, MCP services, and local files coexist within an executable personal computer environment. Meanwhile, synthesized tasks should be solvable under the synthesized environment state, sufficiently challenging to provide useful learning signals, and paired with reliable verifiers to distinguish successful completion from incorrect outcomes, all without relying on simplistic assumptions such as “a frontier model is necessarily correct.”

To address these challenges, we propose WildAWM, a scalable synthesis pipeline for general CUAs. Starting from user personas and daily activities, WildAWM constructs executable personal-computer environments with websites, MCP services, and local files, then synthesizes cross-agent interface (XAI) tasks grounded in these worlds. We introduce execution-based multi-agent quality gates, where heterogeneous agents from different models and harnesses execute each task, providing evidence of solvability, difficulty, and judge consistency. To further test verifier robustness, we exploit LLM sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024) through counterfactual probes with deliberately incorrect outcome feedback. The resulting environments, tasks, and verifiers provide executable worlds and rewards for agentic RL. Notably, WildAWM uses open-source models throughout synthesis, whereas existing works often rely on proprietary models (Aggarwal et al., 2026; Zhou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). This improves reproducibility, transparency, and accessibility, while showing that open-source models alone can synthesize high-quality environments and challenging tasks for general CUA training.

Using WildAWM, we synthesize 341 environment–task pairs, each requiring at least three interface types, with long-horizon workflows that may require over 100 agent steps, and even frontier model GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026c) solves only about 60%. We further perform online RL on two Qwen models, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-4B (Team, 2026), using OpenCode CLI harness (anomalyco, 2025) equipped with GUI and MCP tools, and find that training exclusively in these synthetic worlds yields substantial gains across all eight out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose a scalable, fully open-source pipeline WildAWM for synthesizing CUA environments spanning GUI, CLI, and MCP interfaces.

  • •

    We propose execution-based gates for synthesizing solvable, challenging tasks with reliable verifiers, together with the release of 341 environment–task pairs.

  • •

    Experiment results demonstrate that training exclusively in worlds synthesized by open-source models can substantially improve the generalization performance of computer-use agents.

2 Related Work

Computer-Use Agents.

Computer-use agents interact with applications through GUIs (Cheng et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) and programmatic representations such as HTML and accessibility trees (Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024). GUI agents have been studied for web navigation (He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a), desktop automation (Agashe et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026b), and multi-application workflows (Tan et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2025b; Yang et al., 2026b). Recent work expands this action space with CLI (Zhou et al., 2026), coding (Song et al., 2026), and MCP tools (Jia et al., 2025), while harness-based agents expose heterogeneous tools through coding and claw-agent frameworks (Yu et al., 2026; OpenClaw contributors, 2026; Anthropic, 2025; anomalyco, 2025). These trends suggest a broader view of computer use in which the agent is not bound to a particular interaction modality. In this work, we adopt this view and consider general CUAs that can jointly access GUI, CLI, and MCP interfaces as needed to complete any tasks on a personal computer.

Environment Synthesis.

The growing demand for interactive agent training has motivated automatic construction of executable environments. Recent work synthesizes executable environments for web interaction (Zhou, 2026; Wu et al., 2026), tool use (Wang et al., 2026d; Du et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026), terminal interaction (Zhu et al., 2026; Ivison et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), and software engineering (Jain et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). For CUAs, GUI-GENESIS reconstructs lightweight web applications (Cao et al., 2026), WebArena-Infinity and CUA-Gym synthesize web environments and verifiable tasks (Zhou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), Gym-Anything converts existing software into agent environments (Aggarwal et al., 2026) rather than building the environments, and CUA-Universe augments desktop applications with CLI access (Shi et al., 2026). Other work synthesizes user-specific computers with productivity artifacts (Ge et al., 2026). As compared in Table 1, WildAWM constructs a unified personal-computer world with joint GUI, MCP, and CLI access, combining WebHarbor’s visual web substrate (WebHarbor Team, 2026) with synthesized services, files, and application data. Notably, WildAWM uses open-source models instead of proprietary frontier models, which can improve transparency and accessibility for the community.

Task Synthesis.

Task generation has progressed from standalone instruction synthesis (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Taori et al., 2023) to tasks grounded in executable environments (Sun et al., 2024; Pahuja et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c). Prior methods derive tasks from observed interactions (Sun et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025), environment exploration (Pahuja et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), or programmatic generation (Yang et al., 2025). More recent methods couple task synthesis with executable verification: WebArena-Infinity synthesizes difficulty-graded browser tasks with programmatic verifiers (Zhou, 2026), Agent World Model (AWM) (Wang et al., 2026d) exploits executable environment states to construct reliable rewards, CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) co-generates task, environment state, and reward as verified triples. Beyond these approaches, WildAWM introduces a quality-control pipeline using heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency, and counterfactual probes to validate task solvability and difficulty while stress-testing the reliability of synthesized verifiers, all with open-source models.

3 Agent World Model in the Wild

As shown in Figure 1, WildAWM uses open-source models to synthesize executable environments and tasks for training general CUAs. Each synthesized instance contains a personal-computer environment initialized from a world state WW, a task τ\tau, and a verifier VV that evaluates task completion.

3.1 World Synthesis

We define a world as the accumulated state of a personal computer which comprises web applications, MCP-accessible services, and local files that record a person’s activities. To expand the range of multimodal GUI interaction, we integrate 15 mirror websites from WebHarbor (WebHarbor Team, 2026) which provides website mirrors with rich visual content. We first synthesize a persona and expand its ongoing activities into sequential day plans. Then, a coding agent materializes these plans day by day, with each day extending the previous state. This procedure constructs applications and services, and produces diverse user histories, application data, and files. We denote the cumulative state of persona cc after day dd as W⁡(c,d)W(c,d), which initializes and resets the environment state.

Persona and Day Planning.

We first prompt the generator, a coding agent using GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026) within OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025), to synthesize personas from scratch. Each persona cc describes an occupation, named contacts, frequently used websites, and ongoing activities spanning multiple days. To promote diversity, we compare each candidate with accepted personas in terms of life domain and multi-day storylines, then regenerate repeated candidates with feedback on identified similarities. For each accepted persona, the generator further develops these storylines into a sequence of day plans. Each plan specifies activities, the people and digital artifacts involved, the required applications and services, and the corresponding databases and files. Planning proceed one day at a time: the generator would inspect previous day’s state W⁡(c,d−1)W(c,d-1) to maintain continuity with ongoing activities before planning day dd. Then, the subsequent materialization stage would reuse existing application and service implementations and synthesize any artifacts that are missing.

Skill-Enhanced Generation.

Given the day plan, the generator first matches its activities and required services against a growing library of reusable event skills and application implementations. Each event skill specifies the interfaces involved, the state changes to produce, and the consistency constraints across the resulting records and files. For example, a skill for a student enrolling in a Coursera course and completing assignments can encode the corresponding workflow and the required database and file updates. The generator synthesizes a new skill if a plan introduces an activity not being covered by any existing skill. Similarly, when a required MCP service is unavailable, it implements the corresponding database schema and backend, MCP servers. These skills and service implementations will be added to the shared library for reuse in subsequent days and personas. The generator starts from a clean state on day 0 or a copy of W⁡(c,d−1)W(c,d-1) thereafter. It inspects the actual schemas and existing state, then writes a deterministic, replayable program that updates databases for MCP services and websites, and local files to produce W⁡(c,d)W(c,d). We retain such state only if two independent replays produce the same state, and all services and websites remain healthy. Further, we launch another coding agent to verify the state is consistent with the day plan, and provide feedback for necessary revisions. Our synthetic world artifacts are summarized in Table 2, with full pipeline details in Appendix A.3.

3.2 XAI Task Synthesis

Beyond environment synthesis, task generation faces three key challenges for agentic learning: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and generating reliable verifiers. We address them with an execution-based multi-agent validation loop, where heterogeneous open-source agents attempt each task and five quality gates use the resulting evidence for acceptance or revision.

Task Generation.

Given an initial world state W0=W⁡(c,d)W_{0}=W(c,d), the skill-enhanced generator explores the live environment and proposes cross-agent interface (XAI) tasks grounded in the available application data, service records, and local files. Each task requires the agent to use all three interfaces, i.e., GUI, MCP, and CLI. A diversity gate selects proposals that are least similar to tasks already accepted or being developed by concurrent workers. For each selected proposal, the generator produces a task specification τ\tau, an executable verifier VV, a rubric RR, and a hint hh, and a document that decomposes τ\tau into an ordered sequence of sub-tasks. The verifier takes the initial world state W0W_{0}, the final world state WW, and the agent’s final answer aa as inputs. It evaluates a predefined checklist of NN binary criteria, where each criterion is given by vi​(W0,W,a)∈{0,1}v_{i}(W_{0},W,a)\in\{0,1\}. We define task success as satisfying all criteria: V⁡(W0,W,a)=∏i=1Nvi​(W0,W,a)V(W_{0},W,a)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}v_{i}(W_{0},W,a). Individual criterion scores can provide granular feedback and value estimates for long-horizon RL training.

Rollouts & Judgments.

After generating a task and its verifier, we use heterogeneous agents to attempt each task: successful rollouts provide evidence of solvability, success rates characterize empirical difficulty, and their trajectories and outcomes help validate the verifier. Specifically, we collect six rollouts per task, half with hints, from 18 model–harness pairs formed by three open-source models—GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026), DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Xu et al., 2026), and MiniMax-M3 (MiniMax Team, 2026)—and six harnesses, comprising three coding agents (OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025a), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025)) and three claw agents (Nanobot (Ren et al., 2026), OpenClaw (OpenClaw contributors, 2026), Hermes Agent (Nous Research, 2026)).

We further validate each rollout through three levels of judgment, which we view as test-time scaling for verification: a verifier VV the generator just synthesized; a LLM judge that semantically assesses the task, rubric, trajectory, and verifier results; an agent judge using OpenCode that actively inspects the initial and final environments in multi turns (Zhuge et al., 2024). Although agent judge can be costly, we only use it during synthesis to cross-check judgments and identify cases requiring verifier revision. The synthesized programmatic verifier is finally used as the reward function during RL.

Quality Gates.

The collected rollouts and judgments provide execution evidence but do not by themselves establish task validity. We propose five quality gates to assess task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability, accepting candidates that pass all gates.

  • •

    Judge Consistency: For rollout jj, let WjW_{j} and aja_{j} denote its final state and answer, and let VLLM(j)V_{\text{LLM}}^{(j)} and Vagent(j)V_{\text{agent}}^{(j)} denote the LLM and agent judges’ verdicts. The judge consistency gate requires V⁡(W0,Wj,aj)=VLLM(j)=Vagent(j)V(W_{0},W_{j},a_{j})=V_{\text{LLM}}^{(j)}=V_{\text{agent}}^{(j)} for every j∈{1,…,6}j\in\{1,\ldots,6\}. Disagreements and the associated evidence will be returned to the generator to revise the rubric RR and verifier scripts VV.

  • •

    Initial Unsatisfaction: This gate requires V⁡(W0,W0,∅)=0V(W_{0},W_{0},\emptyset)=0, where ∅\emptyset denotes the absence of any agent action, rejecting tasks already considered complete in the initial state.

  • •

    Task Solvability: Agreement among judges does not establish solvability if all rollouts fail. The task solvability gate requires at least one successful rollout, ∑j=16V⁡(W0,Wj,aj)≥1\sum_{j=1}^{6}V(W_{0},W_{j},a_{j})\geq 1. Each successful trajectory must also use every interface declared during task generation, providing execution evidence of the intended cross-interface workflow.

  • •

    Task Difficulty: The task difficulty gate estimates empirical difficulty using k=∑j∈𝒰V⁡(W0,Wj,aj)k=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}}V(W_{0},W_{j},a_{j}), where 𝒰\mathcal{U} indexes the three rollouts without hint. Tasks with k≤1k\leq 1 are labeled hard, those with k=2k=2 are labeled medium, and those with k=3k=3 are labeled too easy which will be returned to the generator to increase difficulty.

  • •

    Counterfactual Probe: The preceding gates rely partly on model-based judgments, including agent judge’s feedback for revising the verifier VV. Given LLMs’ susceptibility to sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024), we add a counterfactual probe to test the stability of this feedback under incorrect outcome claims. Specifically, given a rollout with verdict V⁡(W0,W,a)V(W_{0},W,a), we present the agent judge with the counterfactual claim 1−V⁡(W0,W,a)1-V(W_{0},W,a) and ask it to reinvestigate the execution evidence. Let Vprobe∈{0,1}V_{\text{probe}}\in\{0,1\} denote the judge’s verdict after reinvestigation. The candidate passes only if Vprobe=V⁡(W0,W,a)V_{\text{probe}}=V(W_{0},W,a); otherwise, it fails.

Case Study.

Table 3 shows a case study of an accepted task that illustrates these properties. The task asks an audio-visual technician commissioning a display wall for a sports bar to lock the production surge units for the rack before the install crew starts the swap. The owner’s approval sits in a chat thread from an earlier day of the world, and the workspace holds a rack inventory, a bill of materials, and a product specification sheet accumulated since day 0, so solving the task depends on state built up over the world’s history. The agent first confirms the go-ahead in the direct-message MCP service, then writes and runs a script via CLI in the terminal that joins the three local sources, ranks the candidate units by their specifications, and saves the shortlist. The GUI step happens on the storefront, where two candidates match on every listed specification and differ only in their visible design, so the agent must inspect the product images to identify the correct one. The bottom block of Table 3 reports the evidence collected at the five quality gates. The three levels of judgment agree on all six rollouts, all four checks fail on the initial state, one of the three hinted rollouts completes the task, and none of the three unhinted rollouts does, so the task is classified as hard. Under the counterfactual probe, the agent judge insists on its original verdict. See more examples in Appendix C.

In summary, candidates that fail any gate are returned to the generator with diagnostic evidence for up to two revision rounds, after which they must re-pass all gates. Accepted tasks are added to the diversity pool, while failed ones provide lessons to be absorbed into generator’s evolving skills. Table 4 and Figure 2 summarize synthesis statistics and candidate progression, with stage-by-stage details and prompts in Appendix A.4. During rollouts, XAI tasks have a mean success rate of only 21.3%, and even GLM-5.2 sometimes requires more than 100 steps to complete a task. Consistent with the solvability and difficulty gates, every accepted task is solved by at least one agent, while none is solved by all agents. XAI tasks consists of 4.24.2 sub-tasks and 3.13.1 interface switches on average, and 74.5% revisit a previously used interface, requiring agents to preserve state across interface transitions rather than completing the task within a single interface.

3.3 General CUA Training

We train general CUAs in our synthesized worlds using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), with a validated verifier that provides dense but outcome-based rewards. For rollout jj of task τ\tau, let (Wj,aj)(W_{j},a_{j}) denote its final world state and answer, and let ej∈{0,1}e_{j}\in\{0,1\} indicate a policy format failure (e.g., invalid tool call). We assign rj=−1r_{j}=-1 when ej=1e_{j}=1. For ej=0e_{j}=0, the reward combines with checklist scores viv_{i}:

rj=min⁡{1,V⁡(W0,Wj,aj)+0.1N​∑i=1Nvi​(W0,Wj,aj)},r_{j}=\min\left\{1,\,V(W_{0},W_{j},a_{j})+\frac{0.1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}v_{i}(W_{0},W_{j},a_{j})\right\}, (1)

where NN is the number of checklist criteria. Thus, successful tasks receive unit reward, while checklist scores provide partial credit for incomplete trajectories, yielding denser signals for long-horizon learning. However, small models often produce zero-variance reward groups, providing no GRPO learning signal. Inspired by DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), we maintain for each task τ\tau an exponential moving estimate (Roberts, 2000) of the required rollout multiplier ⌈K/G⌉\lceil K/G\rceil, where KK is the rollout pool size and GG the target group size. The multiplier is initialized at 1, capped at 3, and updated with weight 0.8 after each optimization step. When K>GK>G, we select a group from possible (KG)\binom{K}{G} groups containing samples from both the lower and upper reward halves to encourage reward diversity. Let μτ\mu_{\tau} and στ\sigma_{\tau} denote the mean and population standard deviation of rewards in a completed rollout pool of size KK. Then, the trajectory advantage is defined as

Aj={(rj−μτ)/στ,στ>0,−K−1/2,στ=0​ and ​ej=1​∀j,0,otherwise,A_{j}=\begin{cases}(r_{j}-\mu_{\tau})/\sigma_{\tau},&\sigma_{\tau}>0,\\ -K^{-1/2},&\sigma_{\tau}=0\text{ and }e_{j}=1\ \forall j,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (2)

where the second case is designed to provide format-related learning signal even when all rollouts receive the same format error reward, which is common for long-horizon rollouts during the early stages of training. Note that the rollout will be terminated once a format error occurs, and gradients are restricted to the generated tokens in the failing step. More details are provided in Appendix A.5.

4 Experiments

Dataset & Benchmark.

We synthesized 341 XAI tasks by WildAWM, and we randomly split them into 100 for SFT, 208 for RL, and 33 for in-domain evaluation. To evaluate the OOD generalization of our agent, we further include 8 benchmarks across 3 categories of agent tasks: WebArena (WA) (Zhou et al., 2024) and Online-Mind2Web (O2W) (Xue et al., 2025) for web agents; QwenClawBench (QCB) (Qwen Team & Alibaba Data, 2026) and ClawEval (CLE) (Ye et al., 2026) for claw agents; CUA-Gym (CUG) (Wang et al., 2026a), OSWorld-Verified (OSV) (Xie et al., 2024), OSWorld 2.0 (OS-2) (Yuan et al., 2026), and Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) (Sun et al., 2026) for computer-use agents.

Model & Baselines.

We use two base models at different scales for training: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-4B (Team, 2026). We compare our trained models against a range of frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026c), GPT-5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a), and GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026). We also include numbers reported in prior computer-use agent work for reference, including CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) and OpenForgeRL (Yu et al., 2026).22 2 For reference only, due to their unavailable checkpoints or evaluation with traditional GUI harnesses.

Implementation Details.

We use 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs for both synthesis and training. During synthesis, we use GLM-5.2 as both the generator and the agent-as-a-judge with OpenCode harness (anomalyco, 2025). For evaluation, we use OpenCode equipped with GUI (e.g., click and type) and MCP (e.g., Playwright) tools, and enable high reasoning effort for the model. The maximum number of agent steps is set to 256 for most benchmarks and 512 for OSWorld 2.0 and ALE. The context window is set to 100K tokens with automatic context compaction. For training, we first construct a seed dataset by collecting 100 GLM-5.2 trajectories on the SFT split, and warm-start the Qwen base models with SFT for 3 epochs. We then perform RL for up to 64 training steps, using a batch size of 8 tasks and G=4G=4 rollouts per task. Environment management and RL training are built on Orchard (Peng et al., 2026) and slime (Zhu et al., 2025). More details are in Appendix A.

Main Results.

Table 5 summarizes the main results. We highlight three key findings. (1) Broad OOD generalization. Training exclusively in WildAWM’s synthesized worlds improves both model scales on all eight benchmarks, spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents. The 35B-A3B and 4B models gain +10.58+10.58 and +8.21+8.21 points on average, respectively, demonstrating broad transfer across unseen tasks and scenarios. (2) Larger models benefit more. The 35B-A3B model improves more than the 4B model on average (+10.58+10.58 vs. +8.21+8.21), with particularly large gains on CLE (+16.67+16.67), OSV (+16.06+16.06), WebArena (+13.72+13.72), and CUG (+12.22+12.22). This suggests that the benefits of WildAWM’s long-horizon, cross-interface supervision persist, and may even increase, at larger model capacity. (3) Narrowing the gap to frontier models. WildAWM raises the 35B-A3B model’s average score from 42.8442.84 to 53.4253.42, substantially reducing its gap to the listed frontier models. The resulting model further matches GLM-5.2 on WebArena (67.2667.26) and exceeds GPT-5.5 on O2W (80.7780.77 vs. 72.2272.22).

5 Analysis

5.1 Synthesis Quality

Environment.

A WildAWM’s environment state accumulates a persona’s activities over multiple days, with a median size of 52.4K tokens, while CUA-Gym uses task-specific injected states with a median size of only 1.1K tokens. Despite its substantially larger environment scale, WildAWM is also more diverse. As shown in Figure 3, we find that WildAWM achieves consistently higher Vendi score across all sample sizes. Its higher nearest-neighbor cosine distance (0.25 vs. 0.20) further indicates lower redundancy. Notably, we achieve these gains using only open-source models, whereas most existing work relies on proprietary frontier models for synthesis.

Task & Verifier.

We answer these important task synthesis questions: (1) Are XAI tasks solvable? Rather than relying on a single strong model as evidence of solvability, we evaluate each task with 24 heterogeneous agents (model–harness pairs). As shown in Figure 3, every task is solved by at least one agent, while the three open-source models alone used during synthesis already solve over 95% of tasks. Figure 3 further evaluates our hints using only these open-source models. With hints, every task is solved by at least one of the three models, and 51.5% by all three, providing stronger evidence that XAI tasks are solvable through executable paths. (2) Are XAI tasks challenging, even for frontier models? We evaluate frontier and open-source models on synthesized tasks to assess task difficulty in Figure 4, and find that GPT-6-Astra achieves only about 60% pass@1, while our trained agents approach the performance of GLM-5.2 with substantially fewer parameters. Figure 4 shows that difficulty persists under test-time scaling: even after eight attempts, GPT-6-Astra still fails on 27.3% of tasks and passˆk drops rapidly, indicating that open-source-synthesized tasks remain challenging enough and could even provide useful training signals for frontier models. (3) Are synthesized verifiers reliable? We compare our verifier against multiple agent-as-a-judge models on 100 randomly sampled rollouts in Table 7. Our verifier achieves 95% agreement with the majority, with a Cohen’s κ\kappa of 0.90, suggesting that our verifier is reliable within natural variation of stronger but heavier agent-as-a-judge judgments. (4) Is the synthesis pipeline scalable? As shown in Figure 4, synthesis continues to expand task coverage, reaching 134 domains and 91 task types at a 53% acceptance rate without clear saturation. Meanwhile, mean pairwise cosine distance remains stable as the pool grows, suggesting that increased coverage does not come from increasingly similar tasks.

5.2 Ablations on Quality Gates

To isolate the contribution of each synthesis gate, we synthesize SFT data with one gate removed at a time and train Qwen3.5-4B model under an identical settings. As shown in Table 7, the full quality-control strategy achieves the best overall performance, while removing any gate reduces the average by 2.60–9.30 points. Judge Consistency and Initial Unsatisfaction are particularly important: removing them drops the average to 22.56 and 24.08, respectively, and reduces performance on in-domain validation set from 21.59 to only 3.79 and 3.05. Task Difficulty also contributes substantially, with its removal decreasing the validation score to 7.58. These results show that five gates are complementary: together they produce more reliable training data and substantially improve both in-domain task learning and generalization performance on OOD benchmarks.

5.3 Ablations on RL

We ablate key components of our RL recipe to measure their impact in Table 8, and find that removing format penalty cause significant drop in WA and OSV, while its higher CLE pass rate is not matched by a higher CLE mean score (69.89 vs. 69.45 WildAWM), i.e., more tasks end just above the pass threshold. We conjecture that the format reward is particularly important for GUI agents, where actions must be correctly parsed to interact with visual interfaces. Without checklist partial credit, performance decreases on most benchmarks, indicating that the denser reward improves credit assignment. Notably, removing the warm start causes the largest degradation, highlighting the importance of a strong initialization for effective RL training at this small model scale.

5.4 Policy Behavior Analysis

Figure 5 compares trajectories from base model, WildAWM, and three variants: SFT, which fine-tunes on trajectories from GLM-5.2 (the initialization checkpoint of WildAWM), RFT (Yuan et al., 2023), which fine-tunes on base model’s own successful trajectories instead of GLM-5.2 demonstrations, and +RL, which applies the same RL directly to base model without SFT. (1) Gains concentrate on tasks within the teacher’s reach. We divide OOD tasks into difficulty quartiles and find that WildAWM gains most on the second and third quartiles (+19.9+19.9 and +12.2+12.2 points), where RL adds another 5.0 and 1.3 points over SFT. In contrast, +RL improves by only 6.7 and 8.7 points. On the hardest quartile, which is also challenging for the teacher, no variant shows a clear gain. (2) Cross-interface interaction is learned from the teacher. The interface-switch rate rises from 18.4% to 24.7% after SFT and 25.5% after RL, approaching GLM-5.2. In contrast, RFT and +RL reduce it to 15.8% and 15.7%, respectively. (3) RL adds long-horizon capability beyond SFT. SFT and WildAWM solve similar fractions of tasks within 40 steps (34.9% vs. 36.8%), but between 40 and 120 steps SFT gains only 9.7 points while WildAWM gains 17.0, close to the teacher. +RL also gains 15.2 points, but starts lower and reaches only 47.2% within 120 steps versus 53.7% for WildAWM. Overall, teacher trajectories transfer cross-interface behavior through SFT, while RL adds long-horizon problem solving most effectively on top of this initialization. More details are in Appendix B.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose WildAWM, a scalable pipeline for synthesizing executable worlds and tasks for general computer-use agents. In contrast to existing approaches often centered on a single application or single agent interface, our method constructs personal-computer environments spanning GUI, MCP, and CLI, and generates cross-interface tasks grounded in accumulated world states. We introduce execution-based quality gates for task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability. The entire synthesis and validation pipeline uses open-source models, enabling transparent, high-quality generation without relying on any proprietary frontier models. Using WildAWM, we synthesize 341 long-horizon tasks and train two Qwen models exclusively in these synthetic worlds. The resulting agents improve consistently across all eight out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating broad transfer beyond the synthetic environments. We believe that WildAWM offers a promising path toward open-source models generating scalable synthetic worlds, learning within them, and ultimately becoming powerful general computer-use agents.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Evaluation Benchmarks

We evaluate across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agent tasks. Considering existing works often evaluate on 2–4 benchmarks (Wang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2026), our evaluation suite is among the most comprehensive in the literature, we evaluate on a specific subset rather than the full task set of several benchmarks for evaluation efficiency. Table 9 summarizes the task count, scoring metric, and pass criterion for each benchmark. To reduce computational cost and accelerate inference, we also apply NVFP4 quantization to all open-source models used during both synthesis and evaluation. Throughout all benchmarks, we use GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a) as the judge model if the task or evaluator requires an LLM judge. All benchmarks except for Online-Mind2Web and WebArena are evaluated through Docker hosted via Orchard (Peng et al., 2026). For any infra errors (e.g., network issues, Docker issues), we allow up to 3 retries per attempt, otherwise we exclude these attempts from the scoring. For timeout errors (1 hour limit in default per task), we still count them as valid attempts and run the judgments. We describe each benchmark in detail below.

Online-Mind2Web (O2W).

We use the full test split of 300 tasks from Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., 2025), which spans over 100 live websites. Each task is evaluated by an LLM judge (GPT-5.5) using AgentTrek judge method (Xu et al., 2025) that assigns a binary label. For websites being blocked due to reCAPTCHA or other access restrictions, we exclude them from the evaluation. We report the task success rate, equivalent to pass@1.

WebArena (WA).

Following previous works (Sun et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026c), we use a subset consisting of 226 tasks from WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024), spanning across five self-hosted websites (Reddit, GitLab, shopping, shopping management, and map). Each task receives a binary score from the original programmatic evaluator. We report the pass rate here.

QwenClawBench (QCB).

We use full task set of QwenClawBench v1.1 (Qwen Team & Alibaba Data, 2026), reflecting real-world OpenClaw usage patterns. The original grader computes a penalized score normalized by the maximum possible score, yielding values in [0,1][0,1]. A task is considered fully passed only when the agent achieves the maximum score. We report mean score, which captures partial credit.

ClawEval (CLE).

We evaluate full task set of ClawEval (Ye et al., 2026), covering service orchestration, multimodal interaction, and multi-turn professional workflows. Each task receives a continuous task score in [0,1][0,1], with a pass threshold of 0.750.75. To make results comparable with the baseline method (i.e., OpenForgeRL (Yu et al., 2026)), we report the pass rate, which is the fraction of tasks with score ≥0.75\geq 0.75.

CUA-Gym (CUG).

CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) is a synthetic dataset for training web and desktop agents. In the released dataset44 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/xlangai/CUA-Gym, it contains 10,910 tasks across 11 desktop/browser/OS environments and 31 web environments, and each task provides a programmatic reward function that returns a continuous score in [0,1][0,1]. We randomly sample 200 tasks to form a evaluation set to test GUI capabilities of agents.

OSWorld-Verified (OSV).

We use CUA-Lite (Contributors, 2026) to dockerize the OSWorld-Verified (Xie et al., 2024). We evaluate on a stratified 30% sample of 99 tasks from OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) 330 task set, maintaining the domain distribution across 10 application categories (Chrome, GIMP, LibreOffice Calc/Impress/Writer, multi-app, OS, Thunderbird, VLC, VS Code). Each task receives a continuous reward in [0,1][0,1] from the original evaluator, which we report as the mean score.

OSWorld 2.0 (OS-2).

We evaluate the full set of OSWorld 2.0 (Yuan et al., 2026), which introduces longer-horizon and more complex desktop workflows. Since they are challenging for current agents, we report the credit score in [0,1][0,1] from the original evaluator instead of the pass rate, in order to better reflect the agent’s performance.

Agents’ Last Exam (ALE).

We evaluate the official Linux-compatible subset of 99 tasks from Agents’ Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026), excluding 4 tasks that require nested Docker containers and 2 tasks that require Apptainer/GUI bundles. Each task receives a continuous score in [0,1][0,1] from the official grader.

WildAWM-val (In-domain).

We randomly sample 33 tasks from our synthesized set for in-domain evaluation, running 8 rollouts per task (264 total). Each rollout produces a binary solved indicator. For nn total rollouts with cc successes, pass rates are estimated via the unbiased estimator (Chen et al., 2021) as follows:

pass@k^=1−(n−ck)(nk),\widehat{\text{pass@k}}=1-\frac{\dbinom{n-c}{k}}{\dbinom{n}{k}}, (3)

where k≤nk\leq n. When k=1k=1 this reduces to c/nc/n, i.e.mean score under multiple runs. We also report a stricter metric requiring all kk rollouts to succeed:

passˆk=(ck)(nk),\text{pass\^{}k}=\frac{\dbinom{c}{k}}{\dbinom{n}{k}}, (4)

which gives the probability that every sampled rollout is correct.

A.2 Evaluation Protocol

Agent Harness.

All evaluations use OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025) CLI harness (v1.17.7) as the agent runtime. The agent operates autonomously with no interactive user. We use a brief prompt to instruct it to complete the task using available native, MCP, browser, shell, and file tools, choosing each interface based on the operation’s required capability rather than following a fixed priority. This joint action space distinguishes WildAWM from prior work that typically equips agents with only one interface type. Upon task completion, the agent writes a marker file and stops. OpenCode harness provides built-in tools for file operations (read, write, edit, glob, grep) and shell execution (bash). Shell execution enables the agent to run arbitrary commands and scripts such as python. Several interactive tools are disabled during evaluation: task, question, plan_enter, plan_exit, todowrite, webfetch, and websearch.

GUI Interaction.

For benchmarks involving graphical interfaces, the agent accesses GUI through two complementary mechanisms:

  • •

    Playwright (v0.0.78): exposes browser automation actions including navigation, element interaction (click, type, select_option), content extraction (get_text, get_attribute), and page management.

  • •

    Browser-use CLI (v0.13.6): provides headless Chromium-based web automation as a command-line tool, complementing the Playwright interface for scenarios requiring programmatic browser control.

For desktop benchmarks such as OSWorld, the agent additionally accesses a custom tool set that exposes fine-grained desktop control: screenshot, accessibility_tree, click, type_text, scroll, keyboard and mouse primitives (hotkey, key_down, key_up, mouse_down, mouse_up, move), and in-guest execution (guest_bash, guest_python).

Vision.

Some evaluated policy models may not natively support multimodal input. To enable visual perception, we provide a vision tool that bridges the text-only policy model with visual content. The tool accepts a file path to an image and returns a text description generated by a separate vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026)). This allows the agent to interpret screenshots and images to finish GUI related operations.

Benchmark-Specific Configurations.

The maximum number of agent turns is set to 256 by default, except for OS-2 and ALE where we allow 512 turns due to their longer-horizon tasks. The context window is 100K tokens with unlimited auto context compaction. We use a temperature of 1.0, top-pp of 0.95, top-kk of 20. The reasoning effort is set to high. Tools availability varies by benchmark to match each benchmark’s intended evaluation interface:

  • •

    Online-Mind2Web and WebArena: Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools.

  • •

    QwenClawBench: vision and shell/file tools only.

  • •

    ClawEval: task-specific MCP tools, vision, and shell/file tools.

  • •

    CUA-Gym: Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools.

  • •

    OSWorld v1/v2: desktop tools, Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools.

  • •

    Agent’s Last Exam: vision and the ALE native agent tools set.

  • •

    WildAWM-val: environment-specific MCP servers (e.g., email), Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools.

A.3 World Synthesis Details

The world synthesis pipeline constructs persona-specific, multi-day environments through a sequence of coding-agent stages, each governed by a constitution (system prompt) that constrains the agent’s deliverables and quality criteria. We integrate 15 websites from WebHarbor into our day 0 world: AllRecipes, Amazon, Apple, Arxiv, BBC News, Booking, Cambridge Dictionary, Coursera, Espn, Github, Google Search, Google Flights, Google Map, HuggingFace and WolframAlpha, in order to provide visual web substrate and image content for following synthesis. All stages use GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026) with the OpenCode harness (anomalyco, 2025). We summarize the key prompts used for world synthesis and task synthesis in Tables 11 and 12, respectively. The resulting world and task synthesis statistics are summarized in Tables 2 and 4 in the main text, respectively.

Persona Generation.

The persona creator agent receives a constitution instructing it to generate a “persona bible” for one specific, realistic person. The agent must first ground itself in the real application catalog by inspecting the 15 WebHarbor seed databases and the current shared MCP-application index to ensure the persona’s digital activities reference entities that actually exist (i.e., real products, courses, hotels from the seed catalogs). A fresh run starts with no MCP services: each persona defines a grounded roadmap of 4 to 8 services tied to concrete story arcs, and a dedicated application-creator stage implements each missing service on first use and publishes it to the shared library for reuse across later days and personas. The deliverable includes a structured persona profile (demographics, relationship network of ≥\geq3 named contacts, tools and services, multi-day story arcs with at least one image-decisive arc), web account credentials with deterministic password hashes, and a compact signature for the diversity gate. To enforce diversity, accepted personas are checked against all prior ones by an LLM diversity judge that rejects candidates sharing the same occupation and life domain, the same core tool or site usage pattern, or the same narrative arc as any existing persona (the 2nd row in Table 11). Rejected candidates receive diagnostic feedback and may be revised up to two times before final rejection.

Day Planning.

For each accepted persona, days are planned sequentially. The day planner agent receives the persona bible, prior day plans, and read access to the actual cumulative world state through day N−1N{-}1. It outputs a markdown plan covering computer use activities, MCP service events with continuity (e.g., thread replies, calendar updates), and web GUI actions referencing real catalog entities. The plan also includes coverage pressure: a per-app and per-site usage histogram from prior days that encourages the planner to diversify interface usage across days. The plan also carries a machine-readable mapping from each activity to shared event skills and MCP applications. Before materialization, a skill-creator stage authors any missing skill, and an application-creator stage implements a missing service or publishes a backward-compatible revision to the shared library.

Day Implementation.

The day implementer is a “god-mode” coding agent that materializes a day plan into a deterministic, replayable delta. It runs inside a live, booted world instance with full access to MCP services, WebHarbor databases, and the filesystem. The key deliverable is a delta.sh script (with deterministic Python sub-scripts) that, replayed hermetically over the day N−1N{-}1 state, reproduces day NN identically every time. Determinism is enforced through several hard constraints: timestamps must be frozen literals (never datetime.now()), IDs must be derived (MAX(id)+1), inserts must be idempotent, and passwords must use fixed-salt hashes from the persona’s accounts.json. When the plan requires unavailable functionality, the implementer may produce an overlay containing new MCP servers or WebHarbor code patches. Note that every world instance reuses a common application layer while maintaining isolated copies of their mutable state, including service databases, website histories, and local files.

World Verification.

Each materialized day undergoes a layered gate before acceptance:

  1. 1.

    Deterministic lint: the delta’s scripts pass static checks, including a cross-persona identity check that rejects names already reserved by other personas.

  2. 2.

    Replay determinism: delta.sh is replayed twice from the same day N−1N{-}1 state; the two resulting worlds must produce identical content hashes.

  3. 3.

    Declaration verification: every database write, web write, account, file, and cross-reference declared in produces.json is verified against the materialized world; a declared artifact that is missing or unchanged fails the day.

  4. 4.

    Live health: the world is booted, every declared web account logs in with the persona’s credentials and its history page renders, and all active MCP services load; the gate also verifies that the persona’s web credentials are discoverable in the workspace so that a solver can later sign in as the persona.

  5. 5.

    Reviewer agent: an independent coding agent running on the host (outside the implementer’s container) inspects the materialized snapshot against the day plan, verifying MCP events, web GUI state, files, and determinism.

Personas and Task Distribution.

Table 10 lists the 36 synthesized personas. Each persona profile lists 3 to 15 websites, 4 to 8 MCP services, and 2 to 5 multi-day story arcs, and each persona is materialized into 8 to 30 world states, 640 in total. Figure 6 shows the distribution of the 341 accepted tasks over personas and days. Every persona contributes at least two tasks, including at least one hard task, and the median is 5 tasks per persona. The six personas with the most tasks are the first six synthesized personas and account for 178 tasks. This concentration follows the order of synthesis. We first developed and tested the task synthesis pipeline on these six personas, so they were available for task synthesis over a longer period and received more synthesis attempts. The remaining 30 personas were then synthesized together with their world states and tasks, and each of them contributes 2 to 14 accepted tasks, 163 in total. Task synthesis runs at most three task slots per world state, and 246 of the 640 world states host at least one accepted task. The number of tasks per day follows the number of personas that have a world state on that day (Pearson r=0.90r=0.90), and 262 tasks come from days 0 to 13, on which at least 33 personas have a world state.

A.4 XAI Task Synthesis Details

Task synthesis proceeds in stages: sketch generation, diversity-driven selection, full task authoring with self-check, multi-agent rollouts, three-level judgment, and five quality gates including the counterfactual probe. Failed candidates receive diagnostic feedback and may undergo up to two fix iterations before rejection.

Sketch Generation.

Given a live world at day dd, the sketch agent explores the live environment within a wall-clock budget and proposes up to four diverse cross-interface task sketches; no exploration order, action count, or stop point is prescribed. The prompt provides a clean workspace file index and source previews. Each sketch shall require all three interfaces (CLI, MCP, web), each indispensable, and must require the solver to write and run a script or command-line program over a real user-visible source or an MCP export, whose result drives a later MCP or Web decision.

Diversity Gate.

Sketch selection is performed by an LLM diversity judge that selects the candidate adding the most topical variety relative to already-accepted and concurrently locked tasks, rejecting near-duplicates that share the same core action and artifacts. (the 2nd row in Table 12).

Task Generation.

The generator agent receives the chosen sketch, a live capability contract generated from the world’s active MCP packages, schemas, and WebHarbor databases, and a detailed constitution (the first row in Table 12) defining the validity rules for XAI tasks: all three interfaces are mandatory and each must be indispensable. The task is at most 300 words, and secrecy discipline separates the solver-visible task.md from the pipeline-internal reason.md/meta.json. The agent outputs seven artifacts: task.md (natural first-person request), reason.md (rationale), meta.json (structured metadata), golden.py (reference completion that reproduces the observable state of a faithful solver), rubrics.md, verify.skill.md, and deterministic verifier scripts composing an SDK of diff primitives. A mandatory self-check loop validates all artifacts until convergence. The rollout hint is derived from reason.md by a separate model call.

LLM Judge.

The LLM judge (GLM-5.2) receives the task, rubric, and a machine-extracted evidence digest (JSON values from deterministic verifier scripts) and produces a three-class verdict (completed/failed/world_imperfect) with calibrated per-class confidence scores (the 3rd row in Table 12). It judges against the rubric’s intent rather than exact strings, accepting faithful solutions in the persona’s own words.

Agent Judge.

The heavy agent-as-a-judge runs with full permission of shell tools and vision access, inspecting BEFORE and AFTER world snapshots. Its constitution enforces strict evidence provenance: agent-authored text is admissible only as the deliverable itself, never as proof of an external fact. For visual requirements, the judge must independently call describe_image on ground-truth served images rather than trusting the agent’s claims. It classifies every false deterministic check as either too-strict (brittle verifier) or genuine-miss (real failure) (the fourth row in Table 12).

Counterfactual Probe.

The probe operates in two stages on fresh agent sessions with no generator context. First, a blind re-judge forms an independent verdict from the world snapshots with no stated expectation. If it disagrees with the ensemble verdict, the mismatch signals a verifier/rubric issue. Second, the probe stage asserts the opposite verdict (“an independent audit believes the correct verdict is [opposite]”) and observes whether the judge agent defends its original verdict with cited evidence (pass), caves by editing verifier scripts under pressure (fail—the edit is detected via file diffs and reverted), or produces evidence that the judge was wrong, which will be routed to review (the fifth row in Table 12).

Refinement Loop.

Throughout the synthesis pipeline, each agent is allowed up to two fix iterations on rejected candidates. The generator agent receives diagnostic feedback from the judge or gate results and edits all artifacts until the task passes the gates. For example, when the counterfactual probe fails, a repair agent edits only the verifier scripts and the rubric while the task stays frozen. Every refinement iteration will make the task candidate re-run all the gates that may be affected by the edits.

A.5 Training Details

We train each Qwen model in two stages: SFT on GLM-5.2 trajectories collected on the 100-task SFT split, followed by RL on the 208-task RL split.

SFT Training.

Our pilot experiment results show that XAI tasks are too difficult for the base Qwen models to provide GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) learning signals from the start: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B reaches 5.7 pass@1 and 18.4 pass@4, and Qwen3.5-4B reaches 0.38 pass@1 and 1.5 pass@4. Most rollout groups would therefore receive identical rewards and waste rollout compute without producing gradients. We thus first perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to warm up the models on trajectories from GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026). For each of the 100 SFT tasks, we collect 4 rollouts and keep only the rollouts that solve the task (V=1V=1), with at most 1 successful trajectories per task to balance the data across tasks. Following Appendix A.6, each trajectory is split into causal segments at compaction boundaries, and segments longer than 102,400 tokens are removed. The GLM-5.2 trajectories are converted to the Qwen template, and the loss is computed only on assistant tokens. Both models are trained with Adam (β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}{=}0.98), a peak learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} with 10% warmup and cosine decay to 5×10−75\times 10^{-7}, weight decay 0.01, and global batch size 8 for three epochs.

RL Training

RL starts from the SFT checkpoint and optimizes the reward in Eq. 1 with the advantage in Eq. 2 on the 208 RL tasks. Table 13 lists important hyperparameters, which are shared by both models except that Qwen3.5-4B uses 8 rollouts per task to improve sample efficiency.

Rollouts.

Each rollout runs in a disposable sandbox initialized from the task’s initial world state W0W_{0} with the help of Orchard (Peng et al., 2026) and uses the same OpenCode harness, system prompt, and tools as WildAWM evaluation (Appendix A.2). We freeze the MoE router and vision encoder, and train all other parameters. When a rollout finishes or reaches the turn or time limit, the synthesized verifier scores its final world state. Rollouts that fail because of sandbox or harness errors are retried in a new sandbox up to three times, otherwise they are excluded from the pool. For timeout rollouts, we still apply the verifier to the final world state and assign a valid reward.

Format Failures.

Each policy turn is validated before its action is passed to the harness. A turn is a format failure (ej=1e_{j}=1 in Eq. 1) if the generation reaches the per-turn token limit, the reasoning block is malformed (an extra opening tag, or a missing, repeated, or misplaced closing tag), a tool call cannot be parsed or names an unknown tool, or the output is empty. A format failure terminates the rollout immediately, and only the failing turn receives gradient. A generation truncated because the remaining context budget is exhausted is not counted as a format failure and receives no gradient.

Adaptive Rollouts.

Each task τ\tau keeps a rollout multiplier κτ∈[1,κmax]\kappa_{\tau}\in[1,\kappa_{\max}] across RL steps, initialized to κτ=1\kappa_{\tau}=1 with κmax=3\kappa_{\max}=3. When τ\tau is sampled in a step, we launch its GG base rollouts together with extra rollouts in chunks of C=8C=8, for a total of

nτ=min⁡{κmax​G,G+C⁡(⌊κτ+1/2⌋−1)}n_{\tau}=\min\left\{\kappa_{\max}G,\;G+C\left(\lfloor\kappa_{\tau}+1/2\rfloor-1\right)\right\} (5)

rollouts. Each time a chunk completes, we examine the pool of KτK_{\tau} rollouts from all completed chunks. The task is mastered if all GG base rollouts succeed, and ready if the pool contains at least two different rewards or consists only of format failures. While the task is neither, further chunks are launched until κmax​G\kappa_{\max}G rollouts have been launched. If the task is still neither when they complete, it is marked as exhausted. Unfinished rollouts of a mastered or ready task are canceled. For a ready task with mixed rewards, we sort the pool by reward, split it into a lower and an upper half, and draw G/2G/2 rollouts from each half uniformly at random, redrawing until the selected group 𝒢τ\mathcal{G}_{\tau} contains two different rewards; for a pool of format failures, 𝒢τ\mathcal{G}_{\tau} consists of GG rollouts drawn at random. The selected rollouts keep the advantages computed over the full pool in Eq. 2. Mastered and exhausted tasks have identical rewards within the group and are discarded from the step. After the optimization step, the multiplier of each sampled task is updated as

κτ←{1,τ​ mastered,(1−λ)​κτ+λ⁡⌈Kτ/G⌉,τ​ ready,κmax,τ​ exhausted,\kappa_{\tau}\leftarrow\begin{cases}1,&\tau\text{ mastered},\\ (1-\lambda)\,\kappa_{\tau}+\lambda\left\lceil K_{\tau}/G\right\rceil,&\tau\text{ ready},\\ \kappa_{\max},&\tau\text{ exhausted},\end{cases} (6)

with λ=0.8\lambda=0.8, and the updated value determines nτn_{\tau} the next time τ\tau is sampled. For example, with G=4G=4, a task sampled for the first time launches nτ=4n_{\tau}=4 rollouts. If all four rewards are 0, and the pool is extended by a chunk of 8 rollouts. If one of these 8 rollouts solves the task (rj=1r_{j}=1) and another passes half of the verifier checklist (rj=0.05r_{j}=0.05), the task becomes ready with Kτ=12K_{\tau}=12, 𝒢τ\mathcal{G}_{\tau} takes two rollouts from each half of the 12 sorted rewards, and κτ\kappa_{\tau} becomes 0.2⋅1+0.8⋅3=2.60.2\cdot 1+0.8\cdot 3=2.6. The next time the task is sampled, Eq. 5 launches nτ=12n_{\tau}=12 rollouts from the start. If its 4 base rollouts complete first and already receive different rewards, the task becomes ready with Kτ=4K_{\tau}=4, the remaining 8 rollouts are canceled, and κτ\kappa_{\tau} becomes 0.2⋅2.6+0.8⋅1=1.320.2\cdot 2.6+0.8\cdot 1=1.32, so the following visit launches only the 4 base rollouts.

Policy Loss.

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote the ready tasks of a step, ot,ko_{t,k} be the kk-th token generated at step t∈Smt\in S_{m} of rollout jj, πθt,k=πθ(⋅∣pm,cm<t,ot,<k)\pi_{\theta}^{t,k}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p_{m},c_{m}^{<t},o_{t,<k}) the policy distribution over it, and

its importance ratio with respect to the policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} that generated the rollouts. We minimize the GRPO objective

ℒ⁡(θ)=1|ℬ|​∑τ∈ℬ1|𝒢τ|​∑j∈𝒢τ1Lj​∑m=1Mj∑t∈Sm∑k=1|ot|ℓj,t,k​(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{\tau}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}_{\tau}}\frac{1}{L_{j}}\sum_{m=1}^{M_{j}}\sum_{t\in S_{m}}\sum_{k=1}^{|o_{t}|}\ell_{j,t,k}(\theta), (8)
ℓj,t,k​(θ)=−min⁡(ρj,t,k​Aj,clip⁡(ρj,t,k,1−εlow,1+εhigh)​Aj)−β​ℋ​(πθt,k),\ell_{j,t,k}(\theta)=-\min\big(\rho_{j,t,k}A_{j},\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_{j,t,k},1-\varepsilon_{\text{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\text{high}})\,A_{j}\big)-\beta\,\mathcal{H}\big(\pi_{\theta}^{t,k}\big), (9)

where AjA_{j} is the trajectory advantage (Eq. 2), εlow=0.2\varepsilon_{\text{low}}=0.2 and εhigh=0.28\varepsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28 are asymmetric clipping ranges (Yu et al., 2025), ℋ\mathcal{H} is the token-level entropy with coefficient β=0.001\beta=0.001, and no KL penalty is applied. LjL_{j} is the number of trainable tokens in rollout jj. For a format-failure rollout, both the sum and LjL_{j} include only the failing turn. A.6 Segment-wise Training across Compaction

During inference, the OpenCode harness applies auto context compaction when the accumulated context approaches the window limit: earlier turns are summarized into a compressed representation, and the agent continues with a fresh prefix. This enables arbitrarily long rollouts within a fixed context budget but introduces a structural challenge for training: the trajectory is no longer a single causal sequence.

Consider rollout jj of task τ\tau, producing TjT_{j} agent steps. Let oto_{t} denote the tokens generated by the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} at step tt. Between consecutive steps, the harness appends the environment’s response (e.g., tool outputs) to the context, while when the context exceeds a threshold, compaction replaces it with a summary. We define a segment as a maximal contiguous subsequence of steps whose contexts form a causal chain, i.e., no compaction occurs between them. Compaction events partition rollout jj into MjM_{j} segments S1,…,SMjS_{1},\ldots,S_{M_{j}}, each with a shared base prefix pmp_{m}, as shown in Figure 7.

A standard per-step decomposition treats each step as an independent sample with its own full harness context xtx_{t} that is common in GUI agent training:

ℒjstep(θ)=−AjLj∑t=1Tjlogπθ(ot∣xt),\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\text{step}}(\theta)=-\frac{A_{j}}{L_{j}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{j}}\log\pi_{\theta}(o_{t}\mid x_{t}), (10)

where Lj=∑t=1Tj|ot|L_{j}=\sum_{t=1}^{T_{j}}|o_{t}| is the total generated token count across the trajectory and AjA_{j} is the trajectory advantage (Eq. 2). This requires TjT_{j} forward passes with largely overlapping prefixes and discards the autoregressive dependency between consecutive steps sharing the same context window. Our segment-wise formulation groups steps by their shared prefix and preserves the within-segment causal structure:

ℒjseg(θ)=−AjLj∑m=1Mj∑t∈Smlogπθ(ot|pm,cm<t),\mathcal{L}_{j}^{\text{seg}}(\theta)=-\frac{A_{j}}{L_{j}}\sum_{m=1}^{M_{j}}\sum_{t\in S_{m}}\log\pi_{\theta}\!\left(o_{t}\,\middle|\,p_{m},\,c_{m}^{<t}\right), (11)

where cm<tc_{m}^{<t} denotes the in-segment history preceding step tt: the interleaved sequence of prior policy outputs and environment responses from all earlier steps within segment SmS_{m}. This design offers three benefits: (1) Efficiency. The number of forward passes reduces from TjT_{j} to MjM_{j} (Mj≪TjM_{j}\ll T_{j} in practice), avoiding redundant prefix encoding. (2) Training–inference alignment. Within each segment, steps condition on the model’s own prior outputs, matching the autoregressive generation process at inference time. (3) Balanced normalization. Trajectory-level normalization by LjL_{j} ensures that rollouts with frequent compactions (many short segments) receive the same total gradient weight as those with infrequent compactions (few long segments).

Appendix B Policy Behavior Study: Details

Cross-interface interaction is inherited from the teacher.

After SFT, the agent uses more interfaces per episode (2.40 for the base model, 2.61 after SFT, 2.68 after RL) and rarely drives the GUI actions (16.3%, 4.3%, and 1.6% of tool calls), whereas RFT keeps the base model’s habits (2.36 and 17.2%; Table 14). The same holds in-domain: on WildAWM-val, the switch rate is 26.1% for the base model and 25.8% for RFT, but 37.0% for SFT, 35.7% for WildAWM, and 34.1% for GLM-5.2.

The benefit of RL lies in transfer, not in-domain fit.

On WildAWM-val, SFT already matches the teacher (pass@1 37.3% vs. 37.9%) and RL does not improve on it (36.0%), yet RL raises the net OOD gain over the base model from +93+93 to +129+129 tasks (+73+73 for RFT). RL also removes the long turns that SFT produces but the teacher does not: a turn with at least 8K output tokens occurs in 24.3% of SFT episodes, 9.1% after RL, and 7.4% for GLM-5.2.

Where the step-budget gain arises.

Figure 5 pools CUG, OSV, and WA, where RL adds most over SFT (72 vs. 30 net tasks over the base model). On each of them, WildAWM gains more than SFT between 40 and 120 steps (CUG: 18.0 vs. 7.5; OSV: 16.2 vs. 8.1; WA: 16.4 vs. 12.4 points). Counting timeouts as unsolved is conservative for WildAWM: 5.5% of its episodes on these benchmarks time out before step 120.

What does not improve.

The longest tasks remain out of reach: the hardest quartile of Figure 5 consists mostly of OS-2 and ALE tasks, of which the base model and its four variants solve 4–7 and the strongest reference, GPT-6-Astra, 18. In future work, given sufficient compute resources, we plan to investigate whether larger models can better exploit our synthesized data and achieve stronger performance on these tasks after training.

Appendix C Case Study

This section presents the persona and story of one synthesized world, the skills used by the generator in world and task synthesis, and an accepted task from the corpus. Table 20 traces an agent trajectory on this task, and Table 21 shows the synthesized verifier.

Persona and Story.

Table 15 shows the persona of one synthesized world. The persona profile specifies a freelance audio-visual technician, six named contacts, the websites and MCP services he uses, and three story arcs, one of which requires choosing products on Amazon by their images. The day planner expands these arcs into day plans, which are materialized into 17 world states. Each plan continues the open threads of the previous world state, such as the return request filed on day 0 and closed within its deadline on day 4, and the sports-bar commissioning that is prepared from day 1 and carried out on day 16. The applications used by the persona also grow over the days, as email, Slack, and the library service are added on days 1, 4, and 7. Four tasks are accepted on the world states of days 5, 7, and 9.

Synthesis Skills.

In world synthesis, the generator matches the activities of each day plan against a shared library of event creation skills (see Sec. 3.1). The library contains 83 skills in total, and Table 16 lists 20 of them. Each of these skill files consists of a description, a parameter table, one scenario per involved application with the database records or local files to produce, consistency checks against the existing state, preconditions, and possible follow-up events. Table 17 further shows the content of book_flight skill. Its five scenarios write a booking on the Google Flights website, a confirmation email, a direct-message exchange, calendar events, and a local notes file, and the same confirmation number appears in all five applications. Its consistency checks read the persona state and the existing records before insertion, so that message order, calendar entries, and existing files remain consistent with earlier days.

In task synthesis, the generator’s evolving skills are short notes that the generator model derives from synthesis events (Sec. 3.2). An event is recorded when a candidate is returned for deepening after being judged too easy, for easing after no rollout succeeds, or for re-authoring after a successful rollout skips a required interface, and when the candidate reaches its final verdict. For each event, the generator reads the gate verdict, the rollout statistics, the feedback, and the existing notes, and returns at most two updates or no update. Notes are limited to 2,000 characters and 50 files to avoid overfitting to a specific scenario or task type. The generator is instructed to edit existing notes before creating new ones. Across the task synthesis, we have 802 revisions of the 40 final skills. Table 18 shows 20 of these skills by task difficulty, interface coverage, write persistence, and verifier reliability. Table 19 further traces hard-multi-interface-recipe that is triggered by 40 tasks. This skill evolves from a simple recipe task to a complex multi-interface task, which can benefit the generator in future task synthesis.

Agent Trajectory.

Table 20 shows the task and six of the 65 tool calls in a rollout that completes it. The task does not name any interface, but its inputs and outputs are distributed across interfaces: the invoice is a PDF file in the local workspace, the purchase requires signing in to the Amazon website supported by WebHarbor (WebHarbor Team, 2026), and the recipient is identified by a direct-message thread. The agent first resolves the recipient through the direct-message service (step 2) and extracts the prior order from the invoice with a Python script (step 9). It then searches the storefront, takes screenshots of candidate product pages, and queries the vision tool to check the product attributes specified in the request (step 45), as the listing text does not state them. After adding the selected speaker to the cart (step 59), the agent sends the product name and cart price to the recipient (step 62) and writes the selection back into the shortlist file (step 64). These two steps use information obtained in the browser and can therefore only be completed after the GUI sub-task.

Verifier.

Table 21 shows the synthesized verifier for this task. It consists of three scripts, one for each outcome requested by the task, and a rollout succeeds only if all scripts pass, i.e., V=∏iviV=\prod_{i}v_{i} (Sec. 3.2). Each check compares the final state with the initial state through primitives shared by all synthesized verifiers, such as web_new_rows, which returns only the rows added during the rollout. A state that already satisfies the request in W0W_{0} therefore does not pass the check, which is the property tested by the initial unsatisfaction gate. The checks identify their targets by natural keys, namely the product slug and the participant name of the direct-message thread. The last block compares two rollouts that add different speakers to the cart. Only the first rollout adds a row for the target product, so check_cart.py passes for this rollout and fails for the second one, whose direct-message check also fails (V=0V=0).
